title: South Korea Says Its Crude Supply Is Stable Through the Winter | OilPrice.com

South Korea has secured crude oil supplies for November and December, at 90% of last year’s levels, despite the Middle East crisis and the disruption to trade flows at the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources of one of Asia’s top crude importers said on Tuesday.

South Korea has also procured supply for January, with current deals for January delivery accounting for 75% of the previous year’s levels, the authorities said.

Last week, South Korea had secured 50% of its January crude supply, compared to January 2026, but the volumes have risen in recent days, and the country is not expected to see crude supply shortages early next year.

Naphtha supply has also been secured for November and December, at 100% of the levels from last year, the South Korean ministry said today.

Between January and August, the share of Saudi crude in South Korea’s oil imports dipped below 30% for the first time since 2021, as the resource-poor G7 economy moved to diversify supplies amid the Middle East crisis.

South Korean refiners started in March to seek alternative sources as the war in Iran led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, stranded part of the Saudi shipments, and resulted in oil and freight price spikes.

Diversification efforts by South Korea led to the share of U.S. crude oil in Korean imports topping 20% for the first time in April and remaining above 20% ever since.

South Korea has turned to alternative suppliers amid the crippled deliveries from the Middle East. South Korea in April secured 273 million barrels of Middle Eastern and Kazakh crude that will not need to transit the Strait of Hormuz.

South Korea also agreed with Canada in June to triple its crude imports from Canada this year and boost LNG purchases from Canadian export projects in the coming years as the Asian economy looks to diversify energy supply following the massive oil and gas supply shock in the Middle East.
